a history of stronger anchoring. Before multi- agent research workflows became feasible, the main bottlenecks were access to machine-readable scholarly corpora, citation graphs, and interfaces for grounding generated text in evidence. At the corpus level, Lo et al. [74] introduced S2ORC, a large-scale structured corpus that made citation-aware retrieval and document-level text mining practical at scale. At the catalog and graph level, Priem et al. [75] introduced OpenAlex as a fully open index of works, authors, institutions, venues, and concepts, giving later systems a programmable substrate forliterature discovery, citation traversal, and bibliometric filtering. These resources matter because many later “research agents” inherit their apparent capability from the quality of the scholarly substrate underneath them. A first wave of LLM-era work then focused on citation-grounded text generation rather than full research automation. Gao et al.
